context_blurb:
Every living thing needs things from its surroundings: light, water, food, a place to live, shelter and a mate. Ecologists call these resources. When one runs short, living things compete for it, and the contest settles which of them thrive. You can watch it in any crowded garden row.

Competition happens only when there is not enough of a resource for both. Where there is plenty, sharing costs no one anything, however close together the neighbours live. Members of one species often compete hardest, since they need exactly the same things, but different kinds compete too.

Competing needs no fight, and not even a meeting. Desert harvester ants go seed-hunting by day, and kangaroo rats collect the same kinds of seeds after dark. Seeds are scarce, though, and each seed one side eats is lost to the other, so the two compete without ever crossing paths. When ecologists fenced rodents out of some desert plots, the number of ant colonies there rose by 71 percent, and where the ants were removed, the rodents increased.

Plants compete too. A plant makes its own food, but it needs light and water to make it, and nutrients from the soil to grow. Scatter carrot seed thickly, leave every seedling, and the crowded plants all reach for the same light, water and soil nutrients. Most of them end up smaller than carrots given room, because they must share that light, water and nourishment, and many twist around one another. That is why gardeners thin their rows.

In 1934 Georgy Gause raised two kinds of paramecium, the slipper-shaped pond cell, both of which feed on bacteria. Grown in tubes of their own, both kinds did well. Sharing a single tube and a limited food supply, one kind kept growing and thrived while the other dwindled and died out. Two kinds that need exactly the same scarce resource cannot share it for long, and kinds living side by side in nature often use different foods or places.

Ecologists call anything that holds a population down a limiting factor: often a resource in short supply, such as food, water or places to nest, but sometimes a predator or a disease. Great tits and other small birds that breed in tree hollows show how it works. Where felling had left few hollows, ecologists hung up nest boxes, and more of the birds bred there, because the shortage of holes had been keeping their numbers low.

For a crop, the limit is set by the scarcest thing it needs, not by the total. Wheat draws two nutrients from the soil, nitrogen and phosphorus. If a field is rich in nitrogen but short of phosphorus, adding more nitrogen does nothing, because the phosphorus, the scarcer of the two, sets how much the wheat can grow. Carl Sprengel stated the idea first, in 1828, and Justus von Liebig made it famous in 1840. It is often pictured as a barrel built of wooden strips of different heights, which holds water only up to its shortest strip.

A place's limiting factors set its carrying capacity, the largest population it can keep fed and housed year in and year out. A population let loose in a rich new home grows faster and faster at first. As it fills the place, its members compete harder for what is left, so its growth slows down before it reaches the carrying capacity, and its numbers level off near it. Drawn as a graph of numbers against time, that makes an S-shaped curve. A population that does shoot past the carrying capacity shrinks back, but it does not usually die out.

The reindeer of St. Matthew Island made a famous crash, and biologists still argue over its cause. In 1944 the Coast Guard set twenty-nine reindeer ashore there. With no wolves or hunters, the herd swelled to some six thousand by 1963, grazing away much of its winter lichen. Then the herd crashed: nearly all of the reindeer starved when deep snow buried the last of the lichen in the hard winter of 1963 to 1964. Only 42 were left by 1966. David Klein, the biologist who counted the herd, judged that it had outgrown what the island's lichen could feed. Frank Miller and two colleagues, reading the records again in 2005, argued that the herd was still growing fast and breeding well, and blamed that savage winter most of all.
